posts.title: The First Hour: Morning Scaling, Fermentation Rhythm, and Bench Discipline
posts.excerpt: In the quiet hour before dawn at Hallstraat 14, professional breadmaking begins not with heat or flour dust, but with calculated water temperature and precise scale measurements.
posts.content:
At 06:00 in the morning on Hallstraat 14 in Rotterdam, the teaching bakery is entirely silent except for the low hum of the deck oven heating elements. Outside, the city is still dark, and the tram rails along the street remain quiet. Inside, the three four-deck ovens have already spent two hours climbing toward 250°C, soaking thermal energy into their thick stone hearths. For the twelve students arriving in clean off-white aprons, the working day begins without rush or shouting. Professional baking is an exacting trade governed by thermal dynamics and microbial life, and its first lesson is that speed comes only from calm, repeatable order.

Every morning starts at the scales. Before any spiral mixer is engaged, students take digital thermometers to record three numbers: ambient bakery air temperature, flour bin temperature, and tap water temperature. These three data points dictate the precise water calculation required to produce a finished dough at exactly 24°C. A difference of two degrees in water temperature alters fermentation curves by hours, throwing off the proofing schedule for the entire morning. Students record these figures in their bound bench books alongside the morning's formulas. By working through these calculations every day, bakers learn to stop guessing and start reading the environment with disciplined precision.

Once the calculations are locked, scaling begins across the twelve wooden benches. Flour is weighed into stainless steel bowls, followed by precise quantities of grey sea salt, water, and mature sourdough starter drawn from the temperature-controlled proofing room. Founder Elise Vandamme moves between the stations, observing how students hold their bench scrapers and balance digital scales. There is no wasted movement. Flour is kept within the perimeter of the bowl, dust is minimized to protect indoor air quality, and tools are returned to the same spot beside each scale after every use. A tidy bench reflects an organized mind, and in a commercial production environment, tidy habits prevent costly cross-contamination and formula errors.

By 07:30, the four spiral mixers are turning slowly, incorporating water and stone-ground flour into cohesive doughs. The sound in the bakery shifts from quiet weighing to the rhythmic slap of dough against stainless steel bowls. Students stand beside their mixers, watching gluten develop not by timer, but by surface sheen and resistance. When the dough reaches its target elasticity, it is transferred into rectangular plastic tubs for bulk fermentation. Over the next two hours, students execute gentle stretch-and-fold turns at thirty-minute intervals, building structural strength through the core of each mass without degassing the delicate pockets of wild fermentation.

By midday, those early morning calculations manifest as golden, deeply blistered sourdough bâtards rolling out of the deck ovens on long wooden peels. During the 13:00 critique, instructors and students cut into test loaves, evaluating crumb openness, crust caramelization, and acidity balance. What made those loaves successful was not an instinctual stroke of luck during the bake, but the disciplined scaling and temperature control completed before dawn. At Komugi School, we teach students that great bread is the logical consequence of hundred-gram accuracy, sharp observation, and respect for the natural rhythms of grain and fire.

posts.title: Keeping a starter honest
posts.excerpt: Observations on feeding ratios, jar marks and the day-to-day behaviour of a school starter.
posts.content:
Every jar on the shelf carries a rubber band at the level of the last feed. By six o'clock the band tells the story of the night: how far the starter rose, whether it has begun to fall, and how much flour it will need.

Amara Osei asks students to write that level down before they touch anything. The habit is dull and it is the one that matters most when a bakery runs ten starters at once.

posts.title: Reading a croissant crumb
posts.excerpt: What an open honeycomb tells you about butter temperature, folds and proof.
posts.content:
Cut a croissant in half and the whole morning is visible: the evenness of the layers, the size of the holes, the colour of the walls. Tomás Ferreira reads crumb the way a mechanic reads a spark plug.

Students cut one on Friday at the crumb critique and write down two things to change on Monday.

posts.title: What is in the storeroom
posts.excerpt: Flour sacks, grain bins and the quiet arithmetic of ordering for twelve benches.
posts.content:
A cohort of twelve gets through more flour than anyone expects. Lukas Brenner keeps the storeroom list on one sheet: what arrived, what was used, what is left for Friday.

Ordering is part of the course. Students take a turn at the list in week five.

posts.title: The knife roll
posts.excerpt: Why every student leaves with a lame, a scraper, a thermometer and a blank notebook.
posts.content:
The knife roll is handed out on the first Monday. Inside are a lame, a bench scraper, a dough thermometer and a pencil, with a notebook beside it.

By the last week the notebook is full of formulas, temperatures and corrections, which is why we call it the bench book.
